name: Intentionality
statement: Mental states are about things: a belief is about the world, a fear is of something, a thought points beyond itself.
meaning: Intentionality is the aboutness or directedness of mental states, the property of mental states being about, of, or directed at something, whether an object, a property, or a state of affairs. Beliefs are about things, desires are for things, fears are of things, and a thought about Paris is directed at Paris. This technical philosophical term should not be confused with intention in the ordinary sense of doing something on purpose; intentionality is the general representational feature shared by beliefs, desires, perceptions, and other mental states, whether or not they concern deliberate action. The concept has medieval scholastic roots and was reintroduced into modern philosophy by Franz Brentano in his 1874 book Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint. Brentano advanced the influential thesis that intentionality is the mark of the mental: that all and only mental phenomena exhibit this directedness toward an object, which he called the intentional inexistence of an object, so that no physical phenomenon exhibits anything like it. Intentional states have intentional objects, which need not exist, since one can think about unicorns or Santa Claus, and they have content. Intentionality is a central topic in the philosophy of mind, bearing on how the mental differs from the physical and on how meaning and representation fit into a physical world, a problem known as naturalizing intentionality.
mechanism: Intentionality is the feature by which a mental state reaches beyond itself to be about something. To have a belief is to have a state that represents the world as being a certain way; to have a desire is to be directed at some possible state of affairs; to perceive is to be presented with objects and properties. In each case the mental state has an intentional object, what it is about, and a content, the way it represents that object as being. A striking feature is that the intentional object need not exist: one can think about a golden mountain, a unicorn, or Santa Claus, so the directedness of thought is not a relation to an ordinary existing thing, which raises deep questions about the ontology of what thoughts are about. Brentano used this directedness to distinguish the mental from the physical, arguing that intentionality is the mark of the mental. The concept was developed by Edmund Husserl and phenomenology, and it poses a central problem for physicalist philosophy of mind: how can purely physical states, such as patterns of neural activity, be about anything, how can they have meaning or representational content. This is the problem of naturalizing intentionality, and philosophers have proposed various solutions, including Fred Dretske's information-theoretic approach, Ruth Millikan's teleosemantics grounding content in biological function, and the representational theory of mind, while Daniel Dennett's intentional stance treats attributing intentional states as a predictive strategy.

examples.text: A belief is about the world and a fear is of something; mental states are directed at objects or states of affairs.
One can think about a unicorn or Santa Claus, so the object of a thought need not exist, unlike an ordinary relation.

variants.name: Brentano's thesis
variants.text: The claim that intentionality is the mark of the mental, that all and only mental phenomena exhibit directedness toward an object.

variants.name: Naturalizing intentionality
variants.text: The project of explaining how physical states can be about things, via information, biological function, or representation.

whyItMatters: Intentionality is a central and distinctive topic in the philosophy of mind, because the aboutness of mental states, their capacity to represent and be directed at things, is one of the deepest features of the mind and one of the hardest to explain in physical terms. By identifying intentionality as, in Brentano's phrase, the mark of the mental, the concept frames a fundamental question about what distinguishes minds from mere physical objects: a rock is not about anything, but a thought is. This makes intentionality central to the mind-body problem and to the challenge of fitting meaning and representation into a physical world, the problem of naturalizing intentionality that has driven major programs in philosophy of mind, from information-theoretic and teleosemantic accounts to the representational and computational theories of mind. Intentionality also underlies the study of language and meaning, since words too are about things, and it connects to phenomenology's analysis of consciousness as always consciousness of something. Its puzzles, including how thought can be directed at things that do not exist, remain philosophically rich.

limits: Intentionality is a rich concept but its scope and status are debated. Brentano's thesis that intentionality is the mark of the mental, that all and only mental phenomena exhibit it, is now treated as a thesis to be examined rather than a settled fact, and it faces challenges from both directions: some conscious states, such as undirected moods, appear to lack a specific object, so not all mental states may be clearly intentional, while some physical states may possess at least derived intentionality, as in the information-carrying or representational states invoked in naturalized accounts, so intentionality may not be exclusive to the mental. The historical detail deserves care too, since Brentano's original notion of intentional inexistence concerned the object being in the mind and was not originally aimed at the problem of thinking about non-existent things, an association drawn later. And the term must be kept distinct from intention in the sense of purpose.
misreadings: Intentionality is not the same as intention in the ordinary sense of acting on purpose; it is the general aboutness or directedness of mental states, whether or not they concern deliberate action. Brentano's claim that it is the mark of the mental is a thesis under debate, not a settled fact, since some moods may lack objects and some physical states may have derived aboutness. And its objects need not exist, so intentionality is not a simple relation to real things, so treating intentionality as purposive intention, as an established mark of the mental, or as a relation only to existing objects, misreads the aboutness of the mind.
origin: The aboutness or directedness of mental states, with scholastic roots and reintroduced into modern philosophy by Franz Brentano in his 1874 Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint as the mark of the mental.
